text:
I write this from a plane somewhere over the Pacific. Life does this but once in a decade. There are certain divine convergences of events where the window to act is but a pinhole in the spirit realm. There will always be other opportunities. Lower-hanging fruit. Lesser partners will cross your path. Spiritually thin people. Easier people perhaps, yet depth will never be fully met.

What is truly coveted only opens for a short window. Hesitate, and the window closes forever. Risk it all and step through with all that you are, and enter an aligned life with everything you ever wanted and more. Maybe you fail in cataclysmic fashion. At least you can live with yourself that you really went for it.

Inner peace is earned by going for it when it matters. We all wish for serenity.

My alarm goes off at 3:45 AM just outside of Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport. I hesitated in October 2017. I know the pain of having an aligned life taken away by my own doing. Today, I’m going for it with everything that I am.

Her.

Maybe this could only happen after I let go of the people movies warned us about. The types of people we imagine watching us when we make life choices that aren’t fully proven yet. My brother once told me that no one watches movies anymore, and society is missing out on their lessons.

I watched The Fellowship of the Ring (2001) and Frozen (2013) on the 11-hour flight. A similar hidden warning repeats across different genres.

Good versus evil is a mere distraction while another darkness lurks in the shadows:

The townspeople.

They don’t get the same condemnation the bad guys get. But they’re certainly not the good guys either. They get a pass, because they’re meek. And we falsely associate meekness with good. Maybe it took a crisis to learn that the townspeople never stood for me, because they never stood for anything themselves.

Over the years, I’ve collected these types of people in my life. Maybe I was drawn to a version of them who once believed. Maybe they were drawn to my vitality. Townspeople are heartwarming at first. Their living rooms are comfortable, and they have family portraits on the walls. They work hard and send their children to good schools. They’re proud of their towns.

Outwardly, they just want the best for their families and communities. They own businesses where their children pop in after school. They’re the presidents of clubs and organizations. They show their face at local events. But inwardly, you can sense that something is not quite right. They’re seething. At a certain point, it hits you that under their lukewarm mask, they’re quietly rooting against you.

They’re fear-motivated and suspicious. The minute you don’t fit their delicate mold of an upstanding citizen, the minute you’re no longer useful to them, they turn against you. When things inevitably work out again, they shake their heads in disbelief: Dumb luck. Privilege. Access they never had.

They can never be happy for you because they know in their hearts they never went for it themselves. They have to reframe your perseverance to avoid their inner truth:

They’re cowards who took the safe, lesser path precisely when it mattered. We’ve all taken lesser paths. But there are certain windows. Certain divine convergences. Certain pinholes in the spirit realm.

And in those moments, the choice matters.

Having an intentional ordinary life does not mean you’re the townspeople cinema warns us about. I’m describing people who have a proclivity towards suspicion and hide their jealousy under performative modesty. People who see the outside world as a threat to their way of life. People who see really going for it as wrong, because it does not fit their tall poppy syndrome worldview.

I see their small-town preservationist accounts on X. The accounts that played into the fear that infiltrated the world after 2020. They’ll post an image of a quaint New England town with a church steeple and an old schoolhouse with the caption: “Enjoy it while it still lasts.” I want to shake them and say that in 50 years, your small town will look exactly the same. I, too, grew up in a town in Vermont of 820 people. The historical postcards from 1910 show the same houses, only with fields instead of forest. Ain’t nobody taking your life away from you.

If people like you can access it, it’s not coveted.

The townspeople are not your friends. They were never your friends. Watch the eyes of the Hobbit villagers when Gandalf comes with fireworks. Watch the eyes of the townspeople when Elsa accidentally reveals her powers at the coronation. When you announce a big life change, watch the eyes in the towns you live in and grew up in. The gears turn in their minds: You must be independently wealthy to do something like that.

They’re not thinking about you. They’re thinking about themselves.

This gets down to the root of what cinema is. Cinema is created by the great artists of the world to uplift people from the lukewarm abyss of a deeply trodden path. Cinema is meant to touch the outlier children coerced into deeply trodden paths by their families, teachers, and communities.

Reality can be punctured.

You need only relentless perseverance and unwavering hope that things will work out. And a spiritual fortitude to protect your energy from cynicism. Cynicism that starts when the 25-year-old alcoholics complain about the death of the middle class. That their degree no longer gets them a high-paying desk job with a 90s suburban utopia, and a romantic partner.

It’s sad to see young people fall into the political abyss while watching their own life pass them by.

The Internet is full of articles catering to the townspeople: “It’s impossible to live a middle-class life these days.” “The right or the left is responsible.” “We’re headed to a dystopian reality.” “We live in a cultural desert.” “Our education system is failing.” “Our quaint small towns are under threat from outsiders.”

If you’ve ever seen Edward Scissorhands (1990), the most dystopian reality has always been the fear-based plane of consciousness that inhabits suburban life. I spent part of my childhood in a Massachusetts 90s suburb, where many of the parents had high-paying jobs, their children went to good schools, played in the woods, and spent their summers at the beach. Even then, the townspeople felt that their way of life was under threat.

I, too, cannot afford a house in a safe American suburb with good schools. But I can think of few things more torturous than being around people who derive a sense of self-importance from the boards and committees they belong to. The clubs and organizations. The pie fundraisers. The performative apology the suburban moms give for starting with store-bought crust. As though someone who bought your $10 pie is going to complain to you afterwards about your crust. The obligatory fall foliage pictures. Only the spiritually broken would fit such a mold.

Maybe that’s the hard truth of working in the home remodeling side of architecture. Your clients are townspeople. You have to listen to them rant that apartments are a threat to their 1950s version of suburban utopia. You feel the fear in their hearts when they’re sitting across the table from you. It oozes into your pores. It drains your vitality. You feel the relief in your whole body when you push open the office doors at 5:15.

Listening to the townspeople talk turns your mind to mush. You won’t go to a cafe and write for a couple of hours. You’ll go home and stare at your four walls and ceiling. Maybe you’ll dilute your writing voice to appease them. Be performatively modest. Not offer your full self. Maybe this is the end. Maybe you don’t have to really go for it.

Transient labor jobs aren’t much different:

“If I were running this place, we’d have a much better menu.” Followed by a rant about the fancy restaurants they worked in before this.

“The front could use a new paint job.”

“I hope the manager’s marriage fails.”

Townspeople are everywhere at all levels of society.

The seatbelt sign rings, and I’m reminded of the few times I really went for it, and what that took. I think about what it takes to forge your own path. It’s not always easy to tell when you’re actively pursuing an aligned life, and when you’re staring at it through the glass.

You retreat, and the townspeople say, “Good to see you’re back in the fold.” They love it when you retreat. It strokes their sorry egos. “Stop by and grab a pint.”

On the plane, I play Fortune Days by The Glitch Mob. A personal 2014-era classic. Maybe I wanted a confirmation that I could still taste that version of myself in the present moment. The song doesn’t resonate emotionally like it once did. The ever-expanding bubble of life has a way of reducing past risk-taking into a mere blip. I’m not my 24-year-old self in February 2015 anymore.

I play Trên Tình Bạn Dưới Tình Yêu by MIN in the plane lavatory. I do my best to avoid the pee dribble in my brand new shoes. For months, I imagined what this song would feel like when I took to the skies. Perhaps I exhausted the newness of the song on those walks to the cafe in the Arizona desert. I packed my dust-stained shoes with me too. I wanted those shoes to see my life working out. I packed the pillow that was with me on all those sleepless nights.

My short layover in Tokyo was a dream. A delirium state. Body dizzy with tiredness, mind too excited to sleep. Another duty-free shop with the same luxury handbag names and chocolates. The international system is comfortably familiar. Still another 6-hour flight to go. I ask what time it is in Phoenix to know when I’m meant to be sleeping. She knows. As does my phone, still in airplane mode.

I’m looking forward, right?

I arrived at my final destination just before midnight. From the rooftop terrace of my airport hotel, I watch the planes take off. Humidity caresses my arms. That familiar sweet taste of air pollution mixed with tropical, dew-soaked vegetation. I could just stay in this quiet village surrounded by rice fields for a few more days. The cafe across the street has a cute tiny dog. He hugs my leg. I think he wants my fried rice with sausage. I know the feeling too well. The “just arrived” glow. Bask in it too long, and the pinhole closes.

I’m still moving. Still passing through it. It’s irreversible now.

In our first meeting, the uplifting MIN song comes on again. I Shazam it to remember the timestamp. 29 October, 2026, 20:45. The rain cloud stops exactly where we’re sitting. The pavement is still dry to our left, wet to our right. I keep my receipt for the two milk teas.

Crossing the street here with all the motorbike traffic is a metaphor for life. Cross with pure conviction without hesitation, and the traffic gracefully moves around you.

I forgive myself for retreating all those years ago. The townspeople’s coercion is comfortable at first. They’ll tell you when you hit the guardrails, and gently nudge you back into the fold. They’re very kind when you fit their mold. It’s all conditional.

Passing through the pinhole is overwhelming at times. There’s a lot to process. It’s disorienting.

It’s not going to turn out as I expected, but I fully trust in what God has in store for us. He is more powerful than we can possibly imagine.

text: 67/100 Practice six: waking up on purpose. The anchor checks where your mind is. Waking up is what you do when you catch it on autopilot. The moment you realise you've been scrolling for twenty minutes, or rehearsing an argument in the shower, or driving with no memory of the last ten kilometres, skip the scolding. Self-criticism just launches a fresh story in the default mode network. Name it lightly instead, almost with a smirk: "Ah. Autopilot." Then make one deliberate micro-choice. Phone face down. Feel the water temperature. Look at one real object for three seconds. Lucid dream research offers a nice parallel. In the 1980s Stephen LaBerge at Stanford showed that some people can realise they're dreaming while still inside the dream and signal it with pre-agreed eye movements. Later work, such as a 2009 study by Ursula Voss and colleagues, found distinctive brain activity in lucid dreams, including more activity in frontal areas. Lucid dreaming is a niche field and no goal of this book. It does give you a powerful image: you can be inside an experience and know at the same time that you're inside it. That double awareness is the whole skill, and the daytime version is available right now, no pillow required.

Some of the best product marketing doesn't feel like marketing at all. It feels like learning something useful.

#Webflow has built an interesting organic growth strategy around this idea.

Someone wants to learn how to build a responsive website. Another person is trying to understand CSS layouts or create their first portfolio site. They start looking for tutorials and discover Webflow University.

They came to learn a skill, but along the way, they also discover a tool they can use to put that knowledge into practice.

Here's what makes this approach work.

01. It attracts people through what they want to learn.

Webflow University offers tutorials and courses on website design, responsive layouts, interactions, and other web development concepts. These topics appeal to people who are actively building their skills, giving them a reason to discover Webflow beyond a typical product search.

02. The education connects directly to the product.

Instead of learning concepts in isolation, users can see how website design principles apply to actual projects. Tutorials help them understand the process while introducing the platform's practical capabilities.

03. Learning reduces the barrier to getting started.

A website builder can feel intimidating to someone who has never designed a website before. Step-by-step lessons make the process more approachable, helping learners build confidence as they become familiar with the tools.

04. The skills create a reason to keep using the product.

Once someone learns to build a landing page, customize a layout, or create a portfolio in Webflow, they have a practical reason to continue using those skills on future projects.

The clever part is how education and product adoption support each other. People discover Webflow because they want to learn, build confidence through its educational resources, and get opportunities to apply what they've learned within the platform.

For SaaS companies, this is a useful way to think about content marketing.

Your audience might not be ready to buy today, but they could be ready to learn something that brings them closer to needing your product.

When your product helps people develop a skill, teaching that skill can become one of your strongest organic acquisition channels.

AI firm Anthropic, headed by Dario Amodei, is officially heading for an IPO after the company filed paperwork on Monday to be offered on the public market.

"Anthropic intends to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” The number of shares of Class A common stock to be offered and the price range for the proposed offering have not yet been determined," the company said in a press release about the S-1 filing.

The AI company, which is behind Claude, filed with the SEC in June confidentially so that the agency could review their financials. The company was founded by CEO Dario Amodei after he as well as other AI researchers left OpenAI. Anthropic has become a go-to for many companies seeking AI tools in corporate America, including the company's Claude Code and Claude Cowork.

The company has been in a race with OpenAI and Google to become the go-to AI platform. Despite its rapid growth, Anthropic CEO Amodei has come under fire for claiming earlier this year that AI companies need to "pace the frontier" with government regulation. Although he called for a slowdown, citing potential catastrophe, Anthropic does not show signs of slowing down anytime soon.

Anthropic's IPO will likely come just months after Elon Musk's SpaceX hit the Nasdaq as the largest IPO on record, which raised $85.7 billion. TWO DAYS AFTER ITS LOWEST PRICE SINCE LISTING, FEDEX FREIGHT $FDXF ROSE 15% ON A DAY THE S&P 500 FUND LOST 1.8%. REVENUE PER SHIPMENT GREW 10%, AND DIESEL WAS ALL BUT 1.6 POINTS OF IT:

FedEx Freight (FDXF) at $126.04, +$16.35 / +14.91% on Friday.

FedEx Freight sits on none of the Len5 watchlists we weigh and fails the Quality Len5, because the debt it took on to leave FedEx (FDX) exceeds the owners' stake. Friday's buyers paid for a beat against low expectations and an outlook raised only in its adjusted form. Diesel surcharges supplied nearly all of the revenue growth, reported profit fell, and interest on the new debt cost shareholders more than the operating gain gave them. The pricing the stock bought is a promise about contracts renewed since June, not yet a figure. Old Dominion Freight Line (ODFL) reported a far larger real price gain on Wednesday and fell 7.3% for it. Repayment comes before a dividend, which is a January decision.

FedEx Freight is not on the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es, and it fails the Quality Len5 on its balance sheet. Quality wants a profit on an owners' stake larger than the debt; FedEx Freight earned $230M in four months on its own, but shareholders' equity, what owners would keep after every debt is paid, was a $252M deficit at September 30 against $4.42B of debt. The deficit comes from the $4.1B it paid FedEx Corporation (FDX) at $313.28, +$5.46 / +1.77% on Friday, before the June 1 spin-off; FedEx kept 19.9% and sits on none of the Len5 watchlists we weigh, 9% under its June high. What would put FedEx Freight on the Quality Len5: years of retained profit lifting that stake above the debt. Momentum wants a stock at its high and climbing on its own news, and Friday's close is 33% under the June 9 high of $188.46; a climb back through it on the company's own pricing would put it on the Momentum Len5. The two value Len5es want a discount from a durable worth, and a falling 11.7% reported margin on an owners' stake below zero offers none; several quarters of the 15.5% adjusted margin showing up in reported figures, at a price near Friday's, would put it on the Quality-Value Len5. Hypergrowth wants sales growing very fast, and 9.2% growth with shipments down is not that, though growth several times faster would be; it pays no dividend, and one covered by cash flow would start the case for the Income Len5.

- Quarter ended September 30: revenue $2.44B vs $2.33B expected, +8%; adjusted EPS, with spin-off costs stripped out, $1.49 vs $1.36; EPS under standard accounting $0.98, from $1.95.
- Outlook, seven months to December 31: adjusted operating income $695M-$715M, from $605M-$645M; operating income under standard accounting $465M-$485M, from $475M-$515M.

Thursday's report was the first covering months FedEx Freight ran on its own, and Marshall Witt, its chief financial officer, credited the higher adjusted range to "fuel tailwinds and slightly higher volume assumptions." Wednesday's $103.475 low was the lowest since the June 1 listing. Friday's close was the highest since September 15 and first among S&P 500 gainers on ChartMill's session list. SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) at $755.72, -$13.64 / -1.77% on Friday.

Diesel, not price, carried the revenue. The fuel surcharge, an add-on tied to the weekly diesel price and passed through to customers, was about $95 of each shipment's $413, from about $62 a year earlier. June through September:

- Revenue $3.28B, +9.2%; shipments per day 88,900, -1.4%.
- Revenue per shipment $413.00, +10.1%; without the fuel surcharge $318.23, +1.6%; revenue per hundredweight, the industry's price per 100 pounds, without fuel +0.3%.

That money covers diesel, not profit, and leaves when diesel falls.

Reported profit went the other way.

- Four months: operating income, what the business earns before interest and taxes, $383M, -6.1%; operating margin, what it keeps of each revenue dollar, 11.7%, from 13.6%; spin-off costs $127M.
- Adjusted: operating income $510M, +16.4%; margin 15.5%; adjusted EPS $2.15, -24.6%.

Even adjusted profit per share fell, because interest on the new debt, about $130M for the seven months to December on the company's forecast, comes out before shareholders.

The pricing the stock bought is still a promise. John Smith, FedEx Freight's president and chief executive officer, said the company has renewed about 25% of its contractual business since June 1 and "achieved our strongest renewal pricing performance in recent years." Two thirds of revenue runs on contracts that reprice one at a time; the other third gets a 6.9% general rate increase, the list price, on January 8.

Old Dominion Freight Line (ODFL) at $172.56, +$0.21 / +0.12% on Friday.

- Quarter ended September 30: revenue per hundredweight without fuel +5.1%; shipments per day -2.0%; operating ratio, costs as a share of revenue, lower is better, 71.5%.

FedEx Freight's was 88.3% over its four months. Our read on Old Dominion's 7.3% fall on Wednesday: its holders sold a real 5.1% price gain with shipments still falling; FedEx Freight's bought a 0.3% one on the promise of more. Old Dominion is #15 on the Quality-Value Len5, which wants a durable business at a discount; the 71.5% operating ratio is the durable half, and 31 times the past year's profit leaves the discount thin.

Repayment has started.

- September 30: cash $388M; debt $4.42B; owners' deficit $252M, from $497M at May 31.
- Four months: cash from operations $390M; spending on trucks and terminals $151M; $100M of debt repaid ahead of schedule.

FedEx Freight is a profitable carrier whose first independent quarter grew on diesel, whose own prices rose 0.3%, and whose debt keeps it off every Len5 we weigh. January 8 comes before the December quarter is counted, tentatively on January 20: a 6.9% increase on the third of its freight that moves at list price, the first price FedEx Freight sets as its own company, and its first dividend and buyback plan is due the same month.

David "Davy" Crockett, the Tennessee frontiersman and congressman, made his famous motto part of a stand that cost him his political career. Born in 1786 in what is now eastern Tennessee, Crockett served under Andrew Jackson in the Creek War of 1813 and 1814. He entered the Tennessee legislature in 1821 and won a seat in the United States House of Representatives in 1827, presenting himself as a plain-spoken champion of poor settlers. He fought especially for squatters in western Tennessee who feared losing their farms to land speculators.

His break with Jackson came over the Indian Removal Act of 1830. The bill authorized the president to negotiate the removal of Native nations, including the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole, from their homelands in the Southeast to lands west of the Mississippi. Crockett spoke against it and voted no, the only member of the Tennessee delegation to do so. The act passed the House narrowly and was signed on 28 May 1830. Its enforcement led to the deaths of thousands of Native people during forced removals, including the Cherokee Trail of Tears in 1838 and 1839.

Crockett later wrote that he would rather be "honestly and politically damned" than abandon his conscience. He lost his seat in 1831, regained it in 1833, and lost again in 1835. In his autobiography of 1834 he offered the rule for which he is remembered: be always sure you are right, then go ahead. After his final defeat he left for Texas, then in revolt against Mexico. He died at the Alamo in San Antonio on 6 March 1836, which helped turn him into an American legend. Almanacs, plays, and later Walt Disney's films of the 1950s added layers of myth to the real man.

Ewan’s Bloody Shirt

Ewan looked in befuddled amazement as the old washerwoman held up a stick with a wet tangle of bloody tunics dripping from it.

“Here, lots of shirts from strapping young men, what’s been killed in the battle. My, look at this one! Why, isn’t this one yours?”

Ewan felt his blood go icy in his veins. He knew this, suddenly, to be a “Woman of the Night,” a ghost or Shee, bringing an omen of impending doom to himself.

Suddenly, the old woman came forward, her face squinting into a cruel mask.

“If thy darling wife should offer thee bread and cheese from her own hand, thou shalt avert thine own terrible doom. Otherwise, I shall be washing the blood from thy clothes…”
***
“Ewan of the Little Head” was the son of the Fifth Laird of Lochbuie (Iain Og), and was prompted by his termagant wife, known to history as the “Black Swan” (But, the reader will ask him or herself, “What is in a name?”) to press his father for his rightful portion as a Chief of the MacLaines. (As you might have guessed, we’re in Scotland.)

This was premature, and Lain Og refused him, enraging his son and causing him to erupt in a tirade of petty vengeance. Lain Og, to his credit, was having none of it, and told his insolent, petty brat that if he should like to meet his own army on the field of battle, well, then, by all means…

The whole thing started as a result of the dissatisfaction of the Swan to her husband’s paltry, uncomfortable estate. Where it would end was destruction and bloodshed.

To wit:

The morning of the battle, Ewan MacLaine arose before dawn, going out to the court where he was met by a strange washerwoman.

A bent-over old crone, with a warty nose and green complexion, we might imagine. She was washing bloody clothes. He then recognized his own shirt in the tub. He felt his blood go icy, for he now knew this to be an omen of impending doom. He was told by the Shee, the supernatural washerwoman, that, should his young wife, the “Swan,” offer him bread and cheese by her own hand, he might live. Otherwise–

Returning home, he was dismayed to find that he was offered no such morning repast.
***

His horse galloped past the great outcropping of rock. Ewan, despite the dire vision of hours earlier, was elated that his men seemed to be winning the battle. He brought his horse to halt for a moment, letting the animal catch its breath. It was then he heard a scuffling above him.
“Aieee!” came a terrible cry, as the shadow of a headsman’s axe fell across Ewan’s forehead. He reached instinctively for his sword, but it was too late.
His head was carried home by victorious soldiers atop a pike.
***
A black mare gallops past the doomed, crumbling walls of Duart castle. The peasant gardener feels his blood grow chill to see it, as it disappears into a roiling, mysterious cloud of foggy haze. Tall and lean, dressed entirely in black, the phantom rider bodes ill, he knows, for the Chief of the MacLaines–as it always has. It is “Ewan of the Little Head”; or, rather his ghost, come round to haunt the grounds of this ancient dwelling, and foretell of an impending doom come to the family, as a curse. But, the peasant reflects, this name of the “Little Head” was intriguing–maybe even comical. For, you see, the phantom rider hadn’t any head at all!

by American photographer William Klein (1928-2022)
--
📚from 'Moscow' by William Klein, published 1964:

"Moscow... the white stone city... the city of radiant towers... of forty times forty churches... the city of bells, of street criers, of dashing troikas, blizzards, poverty and the lower depths... the city of czars and emperors, of Anna Karenina and War and Peace....

Moscow... the revolutionary city... the hive of plotters and anarchists... the mecca of international communism, site of conspiracy, plot, counterplot and revolution... the Kremlin and Stalin's tortured terror... the midnight arrest, fear, the prisons....

Moscow... originator of Russia's New Look... Khrushchev's Moscow where people smile, the Kremlin is turned into a children's snow festival, and people laugh in the streets... the new Moscow, all wide boulevards and underpasses, neon lighting, and mile after mile of mass-built apartment blocks.

What is this Moscow, this multifaceted city with as many aspects as there are bulbous towers to St. Basil's Cathedral in Red Square? Is it Russian history? Soviet threat? Khrushchev's promise?

Something of each, to be sure, but perhaps even more it is people—nearly 6,000,000 of them crowding into the capital, a throng that streams in from every part of the nation, ceaselessly, despite every effort to hold the increase within limits. It is 6,000,000 people living in a city which numbered only 1,800,000 when revolution struck in 1917. And—but for the mile after mile of new housing built since 1958—living in large part in the buildings that stood in the capital when Czar Nicholas II still reigned.

Every year the remarkable new housing developments, giat kvartali or blocks of buildings, eight and ten stories high, assembled by pre-stressed prefab concrete slab construction, march across the flat open prairies that lap at Moscow's outskirts. But no matter how fast the buildings go up, the humanity streams in faster, until the housing authorities throw up their hands in despair.

Who are the people of Moscow? Are they, as Alexander Blok proclaimed, the Scythians "slant-eyed and cruel" slashing out of Asia across the steppes to the threshold of the Western world? Are they the "dark people," dark in superstition, bowing low to the authority of the highest, be it czar or commissar? Are they the masses of central Russian peasantry, low of stature, broad of hip, sturdy, plodding, enduring, patient?

Yes, as William Klein has pictured them they are all these—and many many more. They are buxom factory girls, swinging down the streets in snug blue coveralls. They are laughing brown-eyed teen-agers with beehive hairdos, whirling away in The Twist. They are stout peasant women with felt valenki, cheap print dresses, and string bags filled with pots from the Moscow stores and white loaves from the Moscow bakeries. They are tired-faced men in workingmen's caps with patent-leather visors. They are white-blond young soldiers with polished boots and trim tunics. They are spade-bearded surgeons with pince-nez and a frown. They are tousle-haired village boys with a bayan and a song. They are strict school teachers, Moscow Art Theater actors, clowns and lion tamers, newspaper readers and chess fans, babies in buggies, old women with canes.

They are Russians, Latvians, Tadjiks, Chukoti, Tatars, Bashkirs, Jews, Ukrainians, Buryats, Mordovians, Ossetians, Armenians, Uzbeks, Kazakhs, Georgians and Azerbaijani.

Once St. Petersburg's chic culture sneered at provincial Moscow. No longer. Moscow takes a back seat to no capital in the world. One million visitors a day pour into its great squares and broad streets—most of them from the periferi, the provinces. But some from almost every nation in the world.

They come from the four ends of Russia—indeed, from the four ends of the earth. You can stand on the wide sidewalk in front of the Hotel Metropol and watch tourists from Chicago drive up in their Volkswagens. Turbanned Hindus with their sari-clad wives push through the revolving doors. Black limousines deposit a trade mission from Hamburg at the door. A svelte Parisian model collides with a Podolsk peasant ploughman, gunnysack over his back. Four Australian tennis players, tanned and lean, watch the throng. In the sidewalk café a dozen languages are being chattered simultaneously. The menus are printed in six languages, including Chinese.

The great statesmen of the world make the pilgrimage to the Kremlin. The embassy quarter has sprawled out beyond the old merchant streets of the Arbat with their great Empire palaces and edifices. New embassies and missions proliferate through the city. The purr of Cadillacs, Lincolns, and Rolls-Royces murmurs in streets choked with roaring ZIM trucks, big Gorky made limousines, fleets of taxis, and chattering little Moskviches.

Moscow is a circular city—a core, the Kremlin; an inner ring, the old white city; the settled area beyond the old city walls, Zamoskrodiye; the area beyond the Moscow River, Zarechiye; the two great boulevards that once were fortified city walls now turning into freeways with limited access, underpasses, overpasses, and all the trappings of Los Angeles. Out beyond the built-up city, beyond the miles of new apartment areas along the Leningrad chaussée and the huge Cheriyomushki developments adjacent to Moscow University in the city's southwest quarter, a circular by-pass highway has been built to relieve the boulevards and central arteries of the endless convoys of trucks that converge on the capital, making it quite literally the crossroads of the nation.

Moscow is a city of hustle and bustle, of surging crowds on the sidewalks, of hordes of peasants pouring into the city and debouching into the wide boulevards at incalculable risk of life and limb. It is a city whose traffic death toll exceeds that of New York (and a traffic law so stringent that the death penalty is often applied to careless drivers).

Moscow has been growing for a long time—slowly and with frequent setbacks. The city dates its founding to 1147. But there had been a settlement long before on the hill that rose at the conflux of the Moskva and Neglinnaya Rivers. Today on that hill stands the Kremlin, once a walled, fortified citadel, surrounded by a moat with drawbridges to give access to its crenelated interior. Before the citadel was built, a rude stockade of wood protected a trading outpost of a petty Slavic baron named Kuchko. In time, Kuchko was killed by a roving party from nearby Suzdal, and the Suzdal princess incorporated Kuchko's settlement into their fief—a poor, isolated forest holding too inaccessible to arouse the envy of other princelings.

In poverty, isolation, inaccessibility was to lie the key to Moscow's rise to greatness. When the Mongol hordes struck Russia in the thirteenth century the obscure trading center of Moscow offered few attractions to raiding horsemen. It was located amid forests and swamps so dense and treacherous that even the Mongol hordes had difficulty in penetrating the terrain. And Moscow possessed little in riches to tempt the invader.

So, while the great cities of Russia were laid waste, their gold and treasure transported east to the great Khan, their fighting men slaughtered, their women taken into slavery, the Moscow outpost was hardly touched. Under the leadership of crafty, greedy rulers, the princedom of Muscovy knuckled under to the invaders and began to grow. When, 350 years later, the balance of power shifted and Russians began to hurl back the Mongols from their land, it was Muscovy that stood at the head and, soon enough, Moscow became capital of all the Russias, seat of Russian power, the throne city of the Great Autocrat.

But even after Moscow began to rise under the reign of men like Ivan Kalita, Ivan the Great, and Ivan the Terrible, it was not all smooth sailing. The city was captured in wars. It was burned down again and again by devastating fires that laid its wooden buildings in ashes. And rulers like Ivan the Terrible often turned their wrath against their fellow citizens, slaughtering them by the thousands.

Yet by the fifteenth century Moscow was the goal and glory of Russia. Travelers journeyed from afar to admire its great cathedrals with their jewel-like domes and turrets. The Kremlin had begun to rise like a fairy-tale city with turrets and redoubts, towers and palaces, many of them built of brick and stone. European travelers found the city primitive but fascinating. Russians bowed down in superstitious awe when the peal of the countless bells sounded forth at Easter.

But it was a city firmly rooted in the great Russian central plain and forest. Its ways were rude and un-European. When Peter the Great strode onto the scene in the seventeenth century, he blamed his nation's backwardness on Moscow. He tweaked the noses of the Moscow boyars and slashed off their beards with his own hand. He took them out of their flowing oriental caftans and garbed them in European clothes. And finally, he took Russia's capital away from Moscow and vested it in the new city he had built at the mouth of the River Neva on the Gulf of Finland, St. Petersburg—Leningrad, as it is known today.

For more than two hundred years Moscow rusticated while St. Petersburg flourished under the fresh breezes that entered through Peter's "window on the West." Moscow sulked, Moscow developed a Russophile, isolationist philosophy. It steeped itself in church mysticism and what it called "living in the Russian style"—a little coarsely, more than a little drunkenly, glorying in heavy foods, tasteless houses, old Russian customs, old Russian tastes. Moscow boyars loved the old Russian Household Rules, with their suggestion that an occasional beating would sweeten a wife's temper. And Moscow merchants loved to "go to the gypsies"—to patronize gypsy cabaret pouring rubles into the laps of the gypsy entertainers, spending a fortune in a week's drunken orgy.

As the decades passed, the dichotomy between progressive, industrial, western Petersburg and provincial, reactionary, merchant Moscow widened. The brilliant writers and composers of the nineteenth century gravitated from Moscow to Petersburg. The young revolutionaries who turned the '70s and '80s of the last century into a night-mare for the czarist court and its police apparatus centered their agitation and their plotting in Petersburg. Moscow was a backwater, a place of refuge when the police chase grew hot in the great capital on the Neva.

Moscow's life was its own. It had its own style—colorful and picturesque. Its streets were squalid and narrow. They were filled with street-criers, hawkers, sellers of pastries, pigs, and ices. The markets were refugees for thieves, pickpockets, and prostitutes. For centuries the Red Square was a marketplace and execution grounds, lined with low cafés, murderers' dens, dens of drunkenness and despair. The Khitrovka market near the Yauza River was a hell on earth where men sold their last rag for a sop of vodka and then lay naked and sorpelled in wooden bunks. It was the life scene of Gorky's The Lower Depths. Moscow was the city of Tolstoy and Chekhov and Repin. It was also the city to which Rasputin repaired for orgies that made those in which he indulged in Petersburg seem like kindergarten play.

In 1812, when Napoleon invaded Russia, it was for the traditional capital of Moscow that he headed, rather than the court city of Petersburg. It may well have been Napoleon's instinct that Moscow, rather than Petersburg, was the true heart of the vast Empire. And while the instinct was true it proved fatal. For the invasion of the Russian heartland and the threat to the traditional, historic capital rallied the Russians to a patriotic fervor that a blow at St. Petersburg might never have aroused. And out of this fervor came the ingredients that spelled Napoleon's doom. He plunged his army into Russia's heart. He defeated the Czar's troops. He captured Moscow and watched the city burn. But the vast land—aroused, defiant, mobilized, and aided by the Moscow winter—hurled Napoleon back and drove him to disaster, from which he never recovered.

It was a lesson ill studied by Hitler when, 120 years later to the day, he marched on Moscow. The defeat of Hitler took longer. But it was more complete. And though Hitler's light tanks and motorcyclists penetrated Moscow's suburbs, his panzers could not equal Napoleon's legions. Despite Goebbels' propaganda broadcasts, the only view Germans had of the Kremlin was from Luftwaffe bombarders.

With all this, for more than two hundred years Moscow was not Russia's capital. Not until 1918, when the imperial German armies seemed to be on the verge of capturing Petrograd, did Moscow regain its national glory. In March, 1918, Lenin transferred the Bolshevik capital "temporarily" from Petrograd to Moscow. He planned to return to Petrograd as soon as the Germans had had passed. Lenin and the revolutionaries never quite trusted Moscow. They preferred the vibrant zeal of Peter's city to the stolidity burgher spirit of Moscow. Lenin moved into Moscow's National Hotel. He didn't expect to be staying long. But crisis followed crisis. The Germans had hardly been pushed back from Petrograd than the White armies took the field. Civil war erupted. Foreign military forces intervened, fighting spread throughout Russia. The Revolution had enough to do keeping its head above water. The return to Petrograd—named Leningrad after Lenin's death in 1924—never came about.

And, indeed, Stalin found Moscow much more to his liking. He did not trust Leningrad and the Leningraders. The dark and mysterious corridors of the Kremlin were more to his style. He slammed shut the gates to the great Kremlin compound. Not until after his death in 1953 were they to open again. He closed down the big department store on Red Square that overlooked his offices. Once again the Kremlin became a medieval fortress, accessible only to the few and the fortunate, guarded by picked troops; to be entered only after triple or sextuple scrutiny of rarely issued passes.

Stalin changed Moscow. He ripped up the streetcar tracks in Red Square. He tore down the ancient Chapel of the Iberian Virgin, whose icon was the city's most miraculous. He smashed the picturesque buildings of Hunter's Row and Mokhovaya, created vast expanses of asphalt squares, and lined their sides with runcen buildings in a graceless style that came to be known as Stalinesque. He tripled the width of Tverskaya Street, christened is for Gorky, and erected a façade of mock-heroin shop and apartment buildings along its lower course. The parks and trees of Theater Square were leveled. The greenery and bridal paths of the Boulevard circles were obliterated and huge arteries created to enable swift deployment of troops to any section of the city.

Under Stalin the city grew steadily. But it grew as a grim, unsmiling city. There were no cafés for idle chatter. And no idle chatter. No trees for casual shade. And no casualness. The open squares around the Kremlin afforded excellent fields of fire against any gathering mob. But no mobs gathered. At the touch of a button an alarm system turned lights red along the careening course of Stalin's limousine as it raced from Kremlin to country villa and back again at 70 miles an hour.

In the heart of the city stood the Lubyanka—one of the world's most chilling prisons, high on a hill a stone's throw from the Kremlin on one of the busiest of central squares, a daily reminder of the terror that underlay the life of Moscow.

All this began to change March 5, 1953, when Stalin died. Not rapidly. But inexorably.

It is the new Moscow, firmly rooted in the old, but growing strongly with new life, new vigor, and new spirit that has been captured so vividly by William Klein's camera. Here is a people that has begun to relax, a people that is strolling the boulevards, newly lined with trees, laughing in the parks, dressing up for the theater and opera, gazing in the glistening store windows, ogling pretty girls, preparing to take the stage, mastering new scientific techniques, writing iconoclastic poems, dancing at parties, shopping, studying, playing, making love, saying prayers, tending babies, and composing symphonies.

The faces that the camera records are a record of humanity. We see in them the crags and crevices, the scars and ruins of the past and its trials—the Stalin terror, the ravages of war, the long, harsh Slavic heritage. And we see, too, the vitality of the young, the tender new generations that somehow spring up from the debris and clutter of the past. They are confident faces. Sometimes serious, sometimes gay. But there is little of mystery, little of suspicion. They do not emanate an aura of fear. They are plain faces—open, simple, with a message writ plain for all to see. It is no secret to one who looks into these eyes that this is a people that has mixed many a complex strain. The touch of the Mongol, the blond Nordic strain, the dark eyes of the Caucasus, the tawny skin of Central Asia, the narrow eyes of Siberia's tribes—there is a trace of all this and more in the faces of Moscow.

We see Moscow in the workaday uniform of factory and office; in the holiday explosion of fireworks and dancing in the streets; the banners of Red Square parades, the pageantry of athletics, the homely tasks of butchering, the gay delight of buying a trousseau.

We see the magic of Red Square, the architectural jewels of St. Basil's, the underground fairyland of the subway, the unbelievable beauty of the Kremlin. The crystal chandeliers of the great GUM department store glitter over the peasant throngs. The National Hotel provides a lace-curtain scrim for the distances of Manezhny Square. Russian children scrawl pictures on the wall and dress like snow bunnies. In the parks the young men play the bayan and the girls dance. At country dachas old men take the sun; young men play volleyball; women look after the cows; grandma watches baby in the park; father hoists his son on his shoulder as they walk through the crowd. Sculptors pose with their statues, actresses at their makeup mirrors, artists with their collections.

Is this Moscow? Yes. That is—it is the people's Moscow. Not the official Moscow. Here are no Kremlin bigwigs. Khrushchev delivers no speeches, inspects no factories. No Communist Party functions are seen, no Agitprops conveying the Party line. But it is there. And if some of the faces there is a guarded look, if some of the eyes hint at reserved depths—then, this may be a reflection of those aspects of Moscow that lie outside the focus of the lens. For Moscow is politics as well as people, and the people of Moscow never forget this. If, under Khrushchev they need not keep the politics of it all perpetually in the forefront of consciousness, this does not mean that they lose sight of it completely. "In Russia everything is political," a wise observer once remarked. This is a lesson every Muscovite learns in the cradle.

Everything is politics. There is a totality about the Marxist philosophy under which Russia now lives that is hard for westerners to understand. It seems unbelievable that a government should concern itself with how its people disport themselves in their leisure time; the style of women's dresses; the kind of music young men play in their jazz bands. And so, when we see the people of Moscow dressing like the people of Paris, London, or even New York; when we see them in their off hours, sitting in parks with their girls, dancing cheek to cheek, taking their pleasure in quiet and conventional ways; when we hear them blowing Western jazz through their trumpets and having a fling at The Twist, all of this has a political meaning. It means that the men who now rule Russia are willing, not so eager, to let their hard-pressed people relax and take it easy. They have lost the xenophobic suspicions that embittered the Stalin era. No longer do they think that jazz bands are subversive—even if they do not enjoy very much what Gorky used to call the "music of fat men." They may still inveigh against young painters who insist on copying the abstractionists of Paris, New York (and Poland), but no midnight knock of the police sounds at the artist's door with the deadly summons to the Lubyanka and Siberia.

And this is the reason—the political and philosophical reason—that underlies the casualness of the Moscow that Klein's camera depicts. It is difficult for us to think of these people being mobilized in the cause of World Revolution. They do not look like men and women who are plotting the overthrow of the U.S. Government, or even the government of some shaky new nation in Africa or Asia. They seem to be content with their own life, their own happiness, their own occupations. A façade? No, indeed. If we talk with the people we find that their minds are filled with mundane concerns—getting a new flat in the buildings going up in Southwest Moscow, finding the proper furniture for their new quarters, selecting a new party dress or shopping for delicacies for a holiday feast. They are planning vacations on the Black Sea or, possibly, a trip to Italy. They are rearing their children, worrying about Sasha's examination marks, hoping to become a ballerina at the Bolshoi or an actor on the historic stage of the Moscow Art Theater.

It is true that their government may have other concerns. But in a total society of the Marxist type such a sharp division of goals and purposes constitutes a deadly contradiction. Thus, we may conclude that, whatever its long-term goals may be, the government shares, participates in, and even fosters the kind of psychology that is manifest in today's Moscow.

Moscow has been many things in its long history. Suffering has been commonplace. Terror has been a daily companion. War, disaster, and famine have laid the city waste and fire has destroyed it time and again. All of this has tempered the people of Moscow. They know that the moments for relaxation, for gaiety, for ease and comfort, are rare and may be fleeting. They enjoy them while they may and to the fullest. Such a moment in history is now occurring. And this is the moment and the Moscow that these photographs depict."
